title: The Modern Dance 38.1 x 54.2 cm. (15 x 21 3/8 in.)
material: gouache on board laid on panel
description: The Modern Dance signed and dated 'Conroy Maddox/'41' (lower right); further signed, titled and dated again 'Conroy Maddox/'The Modern Dance' '41' (verso) gouache on board laid on panel 38.1 x 54.2 cm. (15 x 21 3/8 in.)
provenance: Sale; Philips, London, 2 May 1995, lot 105 | Private Collection, U.K. | | This gouache of 1941 is typical of the works done by Conroy Maddox in the early years of the war. Given the shortage of canvas and oil paint, he had discovered in his parents' attic a whole bunch of drawing paper, which he used to create sarabands and parades of more or less biomorphic creatures with gouache. Most of them are non-figurative, "pure signifiers" without signifieds - monstrous arrangements of frames, horns, cups, eyes, circles and triangles - mixing geometrical and organic elements in each of them, hardly identifiable but all vaguely reminiscent. Colours are bright, which adds to the energy originating in their disjunctive contiguity. Those proto-historic species are the "erring creatures", the "spectres" which André Breton saw in Yves Tanguy's paintings. | | We are grateful to Dr Silvano Levy for his assistance in cataloguing this lot and to Professor Michel Remy for compiling this catalogue entry. |

title: Reclining Nude 11.8 x 30.6 cm. (4 5/8 x 12 1/8 in.)
description: Reclining Nude signed and dated 'Haile xii 39' (lower right) gouache 11.8 x 30.6 cm. (4 5/8 x 12 1/8 in.)
provenance: Marianne Haile | Private Collection, U.K. | | Exhibited | London, Birch & Conran, Sam Haile Retrospective, 1987 | Cambridge, Jesus College (on loan) | | Thomas Samuel Haile is a lesser-known surrealist on account of his early death in a car accident in Devon in 1948. His view of humankind has always been tinged with an aggressive pessimism. His Reclining Nude is no exception, rooted as it is in his obsession with suffering. But underneath this, there is, paradoxically, a force which counteracts and denies it, a belief in the underlying "life of the imagination". The body is elongated, drawn out, organs are no longer in place and arranged on a line, the feminine sex is reduced to a triangle and the nude is being sucked at by a kind of child or succubus reduced to four emaciated members and a laughing face sucking a uterus-like form, as in a reversed birth. The format itself insists on that chaotic composition and on the pressure exerting itself on the figure and the two-dimensionality helps vision become primary again. The nude, a traditional theme in painting (and sculpture) is ironically presented through a process of distortion, simplification and almost de-humanization, as the prey to that process. Haile, a radical Left-wing figure in the ranks of the English surrealists fought all his life against racism, the exploitation of the individual and the degradation of human values. | | We are grateful to Professor Michel Remy for compiling this catalogue entry.

title: Figurehead and a Wheel, Charmouth, Dorset 6.8 x 6.4 cm. (2 3/4 x 2 1/2 in.) (image);
description: Figurehead and a Wheel, Charmouth, Dorset photograph, gelatin silver print 6.8 x 6.4 cm. (2 3/4 x 2 1/2 in.) (image); 8.2 x 7.7 cm. (3 1/4 x 3 in.) (sheet) Negative circa 1934-36, printed later
provenance: With Birch & Conran, London | Private Collection, U.K. | | Exhibited | Punkaharju, Retretti Art Centre, Surrealism in Visual Arts and Film, 16 May-13 September 1987 | | Many of Agar's photographic negatives are now held in the Tate Archives, including for the present lot. | | In 1934, Surrealism hadn't come to England yet, but Eileen Agar's orientation, then, was already definitely surrealist. In this photograph, the feminine figure listening to the wall and the wheel recalling the steering wheel of a ship leaning against the same wall, create a reality of their own, of a definitely feminine nature, while the mast coming out from the right balances them with its protruding, masculine, if not phallic nature, and refers them to their previous existence. While it would be excessive to call Agar's inspiration feminist, it still points to a double feature of her works throughout her whole career: her love of the sea and its permanence as well as her predilection for feminine elements, both being obviously linked. | | We are grateful to Professor Michel Remy for compiling this catalogue entry.

title: God Help all the Leviathans 24.1 x 15.2 cm. (9 1/2 x 6 in.)
material: gouache and mixed media on paper
description: God Help all the Leviathans gouache and mixed media on paper 24.1 x 15.2 cm. (9 1/2 x 6 in.) Executed in 1924
provenance: Valentine Boué | Private Collection, U.K. | Private Collection, U.K., since 2010 | | A celebrated painter, poet, promotor and collector of modernism, Roland Penrose studied architecture at Cambridge and then painting after moving to France where he lived from 1922 to 1935. Penrose moved to Cassis-sur-Mer where he bought a house, Villa les Mimosas, that he shared with the Greek painter Yanko Varda and met his first wife Valentine Boué. It was here in 1924 that Penrose executed the present work which has clear debts to Braque and Picasso's Cubism. | | The inscription at the bottom of this work 'God Help all Leviathans' relates it to an earlier work Pequod from 1923 (see Sale; Christie's, 6 December 2007, lot 62, sold for £22,100). Pequod refers in both subject and title, to a nineteenth century whaling ship that is included in the American author, Herman Melville's 1851 novel, Moby Dick. In literature, the term 'Leviathan' holds various historical meanings, originally the name of a mythical sea monster it later became synonymous with whales. Whilst the ship in this work is not named it is likely that Penrose drew inspiration from this novel as he had done in Pequod. Given that Penrose was a poet, literary significances abound in his work. Both Penrose and Varda were fascinated by this novel (references to it can also be traced in several of the latter's mosaics around this time) and it held a particular personal significance for Penrose in that it charted the adventures of Quaker captains and a Quaker community. Penrose had been brought up in strictly Quaker traditions. His father James Doyle Penrose was a moderately successful Irish Victorian portrait painter and a Quaker while his mother Josephine was the daughter of Lord Peckover, the head of the renowned Quaker banking firm that bore his name. | | Whilst this work is imbued with literal and historical references it also embodies more direct influences on Penrose at the time. The inclusion of a French flag implies an identification with the artist's direct surroundings and it could be suggested the use of sand was inspired by Varda who had begun to include found material such as this in his mosaics and other works around this time. This work has significance in terms of the evolution of Penrose's style. It is a pre-surrealist work from the 'tender' moment when he was innocently living in Cassis before meeting Valentine and becoming closely involved with the Surrealists.

title: Study for 'Nest of Wild Stones' 13.8 x 22.8 cm. (5 1/2 x 9 in.)
description: Study for 'Nest of Wild Stones' signed with monogram and further signed and inscribed 'Mon ami Mesens/from Paul Nash' (lower left) watercolour, pencil, pen and ink 13.8 x 22.8 cm. (5 1/2 x 9 in.)
provenance: The Artist, from whom acquired by | E.L.T. Mesens, thence by descent | With R.A. Gekoski Books and Manuscripts, London | With Piano Nobile, London (as Landscape with Eggs) | With Abbot and Holder, London (as Flint and Eggs) | Private Collection, U.K. | | Exhibited | London, R.A. Gekoski Books and Manuscripts, cat.no.26 (catalogue untraced) | | The present work relates to the assemblage, The Nest of the Wild Stones, a group of four flints arranged by Nash and exhibited at the London Gallery's 1937 exhibition Surrealist Objects and Poems. Nash produced another related watercolour of the same title and date now in the collection of the Arts Council. Like the present work, the composition depicts an arrangement of flints and egg forms, the Arts Council's version set within a sweeping landscape. For the present work, the setting is more ambiguous, but a sense of 'ground' and 'sky' is unmistakable. | | Nash contributed a chapter to the anthology The Painter's Object (1937, edited by Myfanwy Evans and published by Gerald Howe Ltd) titled The Nest of the Wild Stones which details his discovery of the concept and which includes the note 'I have taken the elements that go to make my nest of wild stones: earth, air, and hard, cold stone. But of the nest itself, what is there to tell? My first looked like a sheet of squared paper with a torn edge, stretched across a barren field'. This description so closely matches the present work, which is dedicated by Nash to E.L.T Messens, that they could quite plausibly be one and the same.

title: Composition 19.3 x 28.7 cm. (7 5/8 x 11 3/8 in.)
description: Composition signed and dated 'Mary Wykeham 1947' (lower right) watercolour, pen and ink 19.3 x 28.7 cm. (7 5/8 x 11 3/8 in.)
provenance: With The Zwemmer Gallery, London | With The London Gallery, London | Private Collection, U.K. | | Literature | Silvano Levy, Mary Wykeham: Surrealist out of the Shadows, Lund Humphries, London, 2023, p.98 (col.ill.) | | Mary Wykeham's Composition (1947) comes at a pivotal time in the artist's life. Earlier that year, her father had tragically taken his own life in the family garden, prompting a seismic shift in her general outlook on life, especially in terms of her spiritual mindset. She delved heavily into Daoist philosophy, finding solace and comfort in the serenities of its teaching, and she began to practice meditation daily. | | The present work represents a visual development of this interest, a highly spiritual work, illustrative of the enormous positive development from her initial grief catalysed by her Daoist engagement. The setting can be seen as her family garden, adorned with Daoist-related esoteric symbols, birds in flight up and away from the earth towards whatever in her metaphysical paradigm lied beyond. | | Wykeham's spirituality continued to develop to the point where she was to dedicate the rest of her life to it. She became a nun in 1950, some three years after she executed this work – a move accompanied by the destruction of a significant portion of her artistic output. Composition, in transit from an exhibition at The London Gallery, evaded the cull, continuing to offer a window into Wykeham's emotional and spiritual mindset in such a defining moment of her life. | | We are grateful to Dr Silvano Levy for his assistance in cataloguing this lot.

title: Painting 75.5 x 55.9 cm. (29 3/4 x 22 in.)
material: oil on paper laid to card
description: Painting oil on paper laid to card 75.5 x 55.9 cm. (29 3/4 x 22 in.)
provenance: Sale; Sotheby's, London, 16 January 1986, lot 12 | Private Collection, U.K. | | Exhibited | Penzance, Newlyn Art Gallery, Ithell Colquhoun: Retrospective Exhibition of Oil Paintings, 2-27 October 1961, cat.no.21 | | Literature | Richard Shillitoe, Ithell Colquhoun: Magician Born of Nature, 2009, cat.no.567, p.337 | | The present work is undated, however the extensive use of the decalcomania technique indicates that it can be no earlier than early-mid 1940s and stylistically the nearest comparator is The Arrow and the Serpent (1944). | | We are grateful to Dr Richard Shillitoe for his assistance in cataloguing this lot.

title: Roman Sun 78.2 x 50.4 cm. (30 7/8 x 19 7/8 in.)
description: Roman Sun signed and dated 'Colquhoun/47' (lower right) oil on panel 78.2 x 50.4 cm. (30 7/8 x 19 7/8 in.)
provenance: Sale; Sotheby's, Ithell Colquhoun Studio Sale, London, 24 April 1985, lot 481 | Private Collection, U.K. | | Exhibited | London, Mayor Gallery, Exhibition of Paintings by Ithell Colquhoun, 5-29 March 1947, cat.no.17 | Bradford, Cartwright Hall, 57th Spring Exhibition, 24 March-4 June 1950, cat.no.267 | Cambridge, Heffer Gallery, Ithell Colquhoun: Paintings and Drawings 1942-1953, cat.no.11 | Exeter, City Museum and Art Gallery, Ithell Colquhoun: Paintings, Collages and Drawings, 26 September-21 October 1972, cat.no.11 | London, Leva Gallery, Ithell Colquhoun: An Exhibition of Surrealist Paintings and Drawings from 1930-1950, 29 October-16 November 1974, cat.no.22 | | Literature | Richard Shillitoe, Ithell Colquhoun: Magician Born of Nature, 2009, cat.no.457, p.300 | | | The present work carries an intriguing, enigmatic air. The tropical feel of the palm trees, the ornamental aspect of the foreground and the blazing sun belie a more fundamental, underlying essence – one of untethered energy indecipherable through the jungle of towering, interlocking blocks that populate the background. The maze-like nature of these blocks brings a subtle, enclosing feel of uncertainty and claustrophobia that is relieved as it opens up above the flattened rooftops and in front of the portal-like entrance. | | The massive blocks and the flights of steps, in an environment very clearly of human design and construction yet seemingly bereft of ongoing habitation, feature regularly in Colquhoun's work of the late 1930s and '40s. Whilst largely naturalistic in the application of paint, there are passages of decalcomania to the plantation: the leaves of the palm trees, the shrubbery at their feet and the centre-piece of the courtyard addressed directly by one of several piercing shafts of energy emitted from the sun. The technique, closely associated with Surrealist automatism and more prominent in Colquhoun's Painting (see lot 14), involves transferring paint from a sheet pressed against the surface to give a ribbed aesthetic. Here, the effect is of a veiny, skeletal structure underpinning the vegetation – imagined, larger scale reflections of the more naturally occurring feature that Colquhoun so delighted in emphasising for it's inherently surreal qualities in botanical works such as Anthurium (1936), sold in these rooms 23 November 2022 for £258,600. | | Colquhoun's engagement with the occult, and with polytheistic and nontheistic belief systems, took on new impetus in the decade leading up to this work. Roman Sun is imbued with a mystical sense of this spirituality; the sun itself is deified as it sears the sky and radiates majestically across the composition. In this sense, the work combines some of Colquhoun's most prominent preoccupations and stylistic techniques of this period with a somewhat more Realist element than in her abstract work exemplified by the previous lot – perhaps a more sincere expression of Colquhoun's wider frame of thinking beyond the realm of purely artistic experimentation. | | We are grateful to Dr Richard Shillitoe for his assistance in cataloguing this lot.

title: circa
description: Aphrodite's Handmaiden oil on canvas 30.5 x 46 cm. (12 x 18 1/8 in.) Painted circa 1963
provenance: Private Collection, U.K. | | Literature | Andrew Lambirth, John Armstrong: The Paintings, Philip Wilson, London, 2009, cat.no.704, p.222 (col.ill.) | | Exhibited | Probably London, Molton & Lords, John Armstrong, 1963, ex catalogue | | | The present work can be dated stylistically and thematically to 1963, in close association with Danae (Private Collection), an important work of this period of Armstrong's career. Where Danae depicts a mythological tale, popularised by Ovid's Metamorphoses, of an innocent mother imprisoned and then exiled due to her father's paranoia, Aphrodite's Handmaiden is a reference to a real historical figure, Poppaea. Wife to Roman Emperor Nero in the 1st century AD, Poppaea fell victim to the emperor's infamous rage after a quarrel, and was tragically killed in the process. The work's title derives from the later myth that Aphrodite descended from Olympus in her chariot to deliver Poppaea's soul to the heavens. | | These works come as part of a broader motif in Armstrong's work, that of injustice towards women, seen through the eyes of Antiquity. Further subject matters within this theme include various female figures related to Homer's Iliad, such as Leda, her daughter Helen of Troy, and Agamemnon's wife Clytemnestra. | | | We are grateful to Jonathan Gibbs for his assistance in cataloguing this lot.

provenance: Raymond Coxon and Edna Ginesi, until circa 1990, from whom purchased by the present owner | | Artists Raymond Coxon and Edna 'Gin' Ginesi met whilst studying at Leeds School of Art (alongside Henry Moore with whom they enjoyed a lifelong friendship) and the couple married in 1926. Coxon studied under Rothenstein, and travelled to France with Moore where they met Bonnard and Maillol, before becoming a member of the 'London Group'. Ginesi also exhibited with the 'London Group' as well as Lucy Wertheim's 'Twenties Group'. | | We are grateful to Professor Brian Whitton for his assistance in cataloguing this lot.

title: Pavilion 15.3 x 26.9 cm. (6 x 10 1/2 in.)
description: Pavilion signed with initials and dated 'CH'73' (lower left); further signed, titled and dated again 'Clarke Hutton/1973/Pavilion' (on the backboard) oil on panel 15.3 x 26.9 cm. (6 x 10 1/2 in.)
provenance: The Artist, by whom gifted to the present owners | Private Collection, U.K. |  | Stanley Clarke Hutton is today remembered for his exploration of a number of different avenues in the visual arts. In 1916, at 18 years old, he became assistant stage designer at the Empire Theatre on Leicester Square, a position he held until the venue was taken over by Metro Goldwyn Mayer in 1928. After an intervening trip to Italy that somewhat inspired his dedication to become a full time visual artist, Hutton joined the lithography class run by A.S. Hartrick at the Central School of Arts and Crafts in London, taking over the teaching of the class after Hartrick's retirement until his own in 1968. Using the class as a springboard of innovation, Hutton developed a refined technique of autolithography, something he deployed in collaboration with Noel Carrington at the publishing house Penguin in the production of affordable, illustrated children's books.  |  | It is, however, Hutton's interest in Surrealism that is most intriguing from the present perspective. An influence taken on board at a more mature stage of his career, Hutton started to produce abstracted, geometrically complex compositions that caught the attention of Roland Penrose, a vital figure at the heart of the Surrealist movement in Britain and the owner of the London Gallery at that time. In his later years, Hutton was exhibited by Penrose at the London Gallery, as well as at the Redfern Gallery and the Royal Academy.

description: Graphomania : Blue-Black signed with monogram and dated '71' (lower right); titled and dated again 'GRAPHOMANIA : BLUE-BLACK/1971' (on the backboard) pen and ink, ballpoint, wash and collage on paper laid on card 20.7 x 29.6 cm. (8 1/2 x 11 5/8 in.)
provenance: Sale; David Lay, Penzance, 14 October 2003, lot 305 (part lot), where acquired by the present owner | Private Collection, U.K. | | Exhibited | Penzance, Newlyn Gallery, Ithell Colquhoun: Montages, Gouaches, Collages, 12-24 July 1971, cat.no.36 | Exeter, City Art Gallery, Ithell Colquhoun: Paintings, Collages and Drawings, 26 September-21 October 1972, cat.no.59 | | Literature | Richard Shillitoe, Ithell Colquhoun: Magician Born of Nature, 2009, cat.no.709, p.370 | | Graphomania is a strategy developed by Ithell Colquhoun to short-circuit the power of the conscious by letting the pen go into knots, come back on itself, create whirls, eddies and snake-like figures, all of them being attempts to draw circles to go deeper and deeper into the dark, hidden territories of the subconscious, vertiginous, hypnotic spiralling to the centre of telluric forces, where the imagination can feel the energy which brings together man and nature. | | We are grateful to Dr Richard Shillitoe for his assistance in cataloguing this lot and to Professor Michel Remy for compiling this catalogue entry.

title: Desert Menace 41.7 x 42.5 cm. (16 1/2 x 16 3/4 in.)
description: Desert Menace signed with monogram and dated '74' (lower left); further signed and titled 'ITHELL COLQUHOUN/DESERT MENACE' (verso) enamel on board 41.7 x 42.5 cm. (16 1/2 x 16 3/4 in.)
provenance: Sale; Sotheby's, Ithell Colquhoun Studio Sale, London, 24 April 1985, lot 554 | Sale; Sotheby's, London, 16 January 1986, lot 13 | | Exhibited | Penzance, Newlyn Gallery, 1974, cat.no.83 | | Literature | Richard Shillitoe, Ithell Colquhoun: Magician Born of Nature, 2009, cat.no.754, p.379 | | Many of Colquhoun's paintings attest to her interest in wild, marginal places, such as deserts or the seashore: primeval locations where nature stands untamed. It is a theme she returned to throughout her life. Desert Menace is a barren, timeless space where the nature of the menace is unstated: Colquhoun merely presents a landscape upon which, like a stage set or backdrop, viewers like the shadowy observer on the rocky outcrop, can project their own fantasies and fears. | | We are grateful to Dr Richard Shillitoe for compiling this catalogue entry.

material: oil on canvas laid on board
description: The Sentinel's Midsummer Night signed and dated 'Carel Weight/1943' (verso) oil on canvas laid on board 46 x 109.2 cm. (18 1/2 x 43 in.)
provenance: With Leicester Galleries, London, where acquired by | Lawrence Olivier | Private Collection, U.K., since circa 1990s | | Exhibited | London, Leicester Galleries, Exhibition of Works by Artists of Fame and of Promise (Part II), August 1944, cat.no.129 | | The Leicester Galleries label on the verso of this work reports it as being purchased by Lawrence Olivier. This is believed to be the iconic thespian actor and director, and winner of the 'Best Actor' award at the 1949 Oscars for his lead in Hamlet. | | Olivier was a renowned art collector, and his thespian roots would chime well with the ownership of the present work, representing as it does a scene from Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream. Olivier's collection contained several works depicting Shakespeare productions.

title: Untitled 25.3 x 19.8 cm. (9 7/8 x 7 7/8 in.)
description: Untitled signed, inscribed and dated 'To/dean/E. G-H/Easter 1960/John Banting' (verso) oil on board 25.3 x 19.8 cm. (9 7/8 x 7 7/8 in.)
provenance: The Artist, by whom gifted to  | Edward Gathorne-Hardy, thence by descent to the present owner | Private Collection, U.K. |  | This remarkable composition is based on the dialectical juxtaposition of geometrical shapes and two musical instruments, two accordions, one of them held by grasping hands. Most of Banting's works feature music as the expression of the energy of life - often of a tormented quality - and the deep link with the activity of the mind as epitomized here by the ironic playfulness of colours in the triangles, the top right-hand side one reminiscent of the shape of the accordion. The general distortion and almost writhing of the shapes say a lot about the artist's feelings at this time of his life, when he was almost destitute. |  | Edward Gathorne-Hardy (1901-1978), to whom the present work is dedicated, came of age as part of the 'Bright Young Things' of the 1920s. |  | We are grateful to Professor Michel Remy for compiling this catalogue entry.

title: The Exploration of the First Journey 28.6 x 20.8 cm. (11 1/4 x 8 1/4 in.) (unframed)
description: The Exploration of the First Journey signed and dated 'toni del renzio 28 October '98' (lower left); titled 'The exploration of the first journey' (verso) watercolour, pen and ink 28.6 x 20.8 cm. (11 1/4 x 8 1/4 in.) (unframed)
provenance: The Artist, from whom acquired by the present owner | Private Collection, U.K. |  | One immediately recognizes Toni del Renzio's vast deserted landscapes with a distant horizon in which strange encounters take place and personal tensions express themselves, here through a veiled figure whose eye has been cut out and placed within a frame and whose body is a plank. The two small figures on the ground seem to be lost, echoing the two balls held in the figure's hands - the like of one of them lies on the ground. There is a general sense of loss, of desegregation, of fragility as of someone desperately looking for a refuge, a place of stability. |  | We are grateful to Professor Michel Remy for compiling this catalogue entry. |

title: The Birth of Aphrodite  53.8 x 64.7 cm. (21 2/8 x 25 1/2 in.)
description: The Birth of Aphrodite signed and dated 'W.RONDAS.69' (lower right); further signed, inscribed and dated again 'WILLIE RONDAS/SKETCH FOR/BIRTH OF APHRODITE/9:X:69/La Naissance d'Aphrodite/(premier projet)' (verso) oil on board 53.8 x 64.7 cm. (21 2/8 x 25 1/2 in.)
provenance: Private Collection, U.K. |  | Willi Rondas was born in Brussels, to a Belgian father and English mother, he initially studied Music and Architecture. He took up painting in 1931, enrolling at L'École des Beaux-Arts, Paris. Upon graduating he worked as a restorer at the Louvre, later becoming an assistant to his friends Raoul Dufy and Christian Bérard on stage design projects. It was through them that he came into contact with the patron and collector Edward James who began buying Surrealist paintings by Rondas, a lifelong devotee of Paul Delvaux.  |  | At the outbreak of WWII Rondas served in the Belgian Army. Evacuated at Dunkirk, he transferred to The British Army and spent the rest of his life in England. In addition to exhibiting in London and various teaching posts, he also designed textiles for Jacqmar. |  | Rondas exhibited extensively in Europe and America, his first exhibition at Galerie Le Centaure, Brussels in 1938. Subsequent retrospectives during his life included at Galerie d'Egmont, Brussels and Ben Uri, London, both in 1961. Another was mounted posthumously at Galerie Rutzmoser, München, 1987.

title: The Companion  31.8 cm. (12 1/2 in.) high
description: The Companion stamped with monogram and numbered '4/8' (on the middle leg) bronze with a brown patina 31.8 cm. (12 1/2 in.) high Conceived in 2020
provenance: The Artist, from whom acquired by the present owner | Private Collection, U.K. | | Morris's earliest engagements with three-dimensional art date back to the 1940's and works such as the object painting War Woman 1949 (National Galleries of Scotland). In the 1970s he produced his first sculptures in bronze, such as Fertility Figure (a cast of which was sold in these rooms 16 December 2020). The present work, and lot 44, belong to a series of works in which Morris revisited motifs from across his earlier-two dimensional output in three-dimensional forms. | | We are grateful to Dr Silvano Levy for his assistance in cataloguing this lot.
